module_title: Feeding Guinea Fowl and Quail with Local Ingredients

lessons.title: Nutritional Needs of Guinea Fowl and Quail at Different Ages
lessons.body:
Guinea fowl and quail have different nutritional needs as they grow. For the first 4 weeks, both need a starter feed with 24-28% protein. This high protein supports rapid growth and feather development. You can make a starter mix using 50% maize meal, 30% soya meal, 15% fish meal, and 5% mineral/vitamin premix. For guinea fowl, from 5 to 12 weeks, use a grower feed with 20-22% protein. A simple grower mix is 60% maize, 25% soya, 10% fish meal, and 5% premix. Quail grow faster; they need 24% protein until 5 weeks, then 20% from 6 weeks onward.

At laying age (guinea fowl from 28 weeks, quail from 6 weeks), increase calcium and protein. Laying feed should have 18-20% protein and 3-4% calcium. Use 55% maize, 20% soya, 10% fish meal, 10% limestone or crushed oyster shells, and 5% premix. For quail, add 2% extra calcium. Always provide grit (small stones) for digestion. Without proper nutrition, birds grow slowly, lay fewer eggs, and get sick easily. Adjust feed as birds age; don't feed chick starter to adults as it's too high in protein and costly.

Water is critical: chicks need clean water with vitamins for the first week. Use shallow dishes with stones to prevent drowning. In hot African conditions, birds drink more, so refill waterers at least twice daily. Watch for signs of deficiency: pale combs, thin shells, or poor growth. Mix feed fresh every week to avoid mold. Store in dry, cool place. Use local ingredients like maize, soya, fish meal, and limestone. If fish meal is expensive, replace with 5% termites or 10% sunflower cake. Always weigh ingredients with a simple scale for accuracy. A 1 kg difference in a 50 kg mix can affect bird health. For 100 quail, you need about 2 kg starter feed per day in first week. For 50 guinea fowl, 3 kg per day. Adjust based on consumption; birds should finish feed in 15-20 minutes. If they leave feed, reduce amount. If they seem hungry, increase slightly. Monitor body weight: healthy guinea fowl chicks weigh 30 g at day old, 500 g at 8 weeks. Quail weigh 10 g at day old, 100 g at 4 weeks. If weights are low, check protein and energy levels. Energy comes mainly from maize; if birds are sluggish, add 5% more maize. But too much maize makes them fat and reduces egg production. Balance is key. Always provide fresh water. This foundation ensures healthy, productive birds.

lessons.title: Mixing Your Own Feed Using Maize, Soya, Fish Meal, and Local Supplements
lessons.body: Mixing your own feed saves money and uses local ingredients. You need a scale, a large basin or concrete floor, a shovel, and storage bags. For a 50 kg batch of starter feed (for chicks up to 4 weeks), use: 25 kg maize meal, 15 kg soya meal, 7.5 kg fish meal, 2 kg limestone powder, and 0.5 kg vitamin/mineral premix. Mix dry ingredients thoroughly by turning the pile 3 times. For grower feed (5-12 weeks), use: 30 kg maize, 12.5 kg soya, 5 kg fish meal, 2 kg limestone, and 0.5 kg premix. For layer feed, use: 27.5 kg maize, 10 kg soya, 5 kg fish meal, 5 kg limestone, and 2.5 kg premix. Adjust according to local availability. If fish meal is scarce, replace 5 kg fish meal with 5 kg termites (dried and ground) or 7 kg sunflower cake. Termites are 40% protein. Sunflower cake is 30% protein. But termites lack some amino acids, so add 0.5 kg lysine if available. Soya is best plant protein. If soya is expensive, use 10 kg groundnut cake instead of 7.5 kg soya, but groundnut cake has less methionine. Add 0.2 kg methionine. Local supplements include: dried moringa leaves (5% of mix) for vitamins, crushed eggshells (instead of limestone) for calcium, and wood ash (1%) for minerals. Never use moldy maize; it causes aflatoxin poisoning. Store feed in airtight bags in a cool, dry place. Use within 2 weeks. For small flocks, mix 10 kg at a time. A 10 kg starter mix: 5 kg maize, 3 kg soya, 1.5 kg fish meal, 0.4 kg limestone, 0.1 kg premix. Mix on a clean tarpaulin. Wear a dust mask. After mixing, test by feeding a small amount; birds should eat eagerly. If they refuse, check for stale ingredients. Always provide grit separately. This method reduces feed cost by 30-50% compared to commercial feed. It also allows you to use what you have. For example, in West Africa, use maize, soya, and fish meal from local markets. In East Africa, add sunflower cake. In Southern Africa, use sorghum instead of maize if cheaper. But sorghum has less energy; add 5% molasses. Always keep records of your mix and bird performance. Adjust as needed. This is practical and sustainable.

lessons.title: Using Kitchen Waste and Farm By-Products Safely
lessons.body: Kitchen waste and farm by-products can cut feed costs, but must be used safely. Guinea fowl and quail are omnivores; they eat many things. Safe kitchen waste includes: cooked rice, pasta, bread (no mold), fruit and vegetable peels (not citrus or onion), eggshells (crushed), and leftover meat (cooked, no bones). Never feed raw meat, moldy food, or salty scraps. Too much salt kills birds. Also avoid avocado, chocolate, and caffeine. For quail, chop waste into small pieces. For guinea fowl, they can peck larger bits. Introduce new waste slowly; start with 10% of daily feed, then increase to 20% over a week. Never replace more than 30% of their commercial or home-mixed feed with waste, or they miss key nutrients. Farm by-products include: cassava peels (dried and ground), sweet potato vines (dried), banana leaves (chopped), and brewers' grain (dried). These are high in fiber; limit to 10% of diet. For example, mix 1 kg dried cassava peel with 4 kg maize in a 10 kg batch. Always dry by-products in the sun for 2 days to kill mold and parasites. Never feed wet or fermented waste; it causes diarrhea. A simple rule: if it smells bad, don't feed it. Provide waste in a separate trough, not on the ground, to avoid contamination. Remove uneaten waste after 1 hour. For quail, use shallow trays. For guinea fowl, use hanging feeders. Kitchen waste can supply up to 20% of daily calories. For 100 quail, 200 g of chopped vegetable waste per day is enough. For 50 guinea fowl, 1 kg of mixed waste. But always ensure they get their main feed first. A good schedule: morning feed commercial mix, midday give waste, evening give more mix. This keeps them productive. Watch for health problems: if birds get diarrhea, stop waste for 3 days and give clean water with electrolytes. If egg production drops, reduce waste to 10%. Also, never feed waste from birds or pigs; it spreads disease. Use only plant-based and cooked food waste. Store waste in a covered bucket for no more than 24 hours. In hot climates, waste spoils fast. So collect and use same day. This practice saves money and reduces waste, but safety first.

lessons.title: Feeding Schedules: How Much and How Often for Guinea Fowl and Quail
lessons.body: Feeding schedules depend on age and species. For guinea fowl: week 1-4, feed starter freely (about 30 g per bird per day). Use a chick feeder; refill 3 times daily. Week 5-12, give grower feed 50 g per bird per day, in two meals (morning and evening). Week 13-28, give 70 g per bird per day. From 28 weeks (laying), give 100-120 g per bird per day. Always provide feed at same times daily; birds learn routine. For quail: week 1-2, feed 10 g per bird per day, split into 3 meals. Week 3-5, 20 g per bird per day. Week 6 onward (laying), 25-30 g per bird per day. Quail eat little but often. Use shallow feeders; quail waste feed if troughs are deep. For both, remove leftover feed after 30 minutes to prevent mold. In hot weather, feed early morning and late evening when cool. In cold weather, feed more in afternoon. Water must be available at all times. A simple rule: birds should finish feed in 15-20 minutes. If they leave some, reduce next meal. If they seem hungry, increase by 10%. For 100 guinea fowl at laying, you need 10-12 kg feed per day. For 100 quail, 2.5-3 kg per day. Weigh feed with a scale; don't guess. Use a calendar to track. For small flocks, use a scoop: a 500 ml cup holds about 400 g of maize-based feed. So 100 guinea fowl need 25-30 cups per day. For quail, 6-7 cups. Adjust based on consumption. Also, provide grit separately once a week. And calcium (crushed shells) free choice for layers. Never feed all at once; multiple small meals improve digestion. For guinea fowl, they also forage; if free-range, reduce feed by 20%. But keep supplementary feed. For quail, they are kept in cages; no foraging, so exact amounts matter. Monitor body condition: healthy guinea fowl have full crops in evening. Quail should have rounded breasts. If thin, increase feed. If fat, reduce maize. Keep records of feed used and eggs collected. This helps you adjust. A good schedule saves money and keeps birds healthy. Start with these amounts and tweak to your situation.

lessons.title: Providing Grit and Calcium for Strong Eggshells
lessons.body: Grit and calcium are essential for strong eggshells and healthy digestion. Grit consists of small stones that birds swallow and store in their gizzard to grind food. Without grit, they cannot digest grains well. For guinea fowl and quail, provide grit in a separate dish, free choice. Use clean, washed river sand or crushed granite. The size should be: for chicks, 1-2 mm; for adults, 3-5 mm. Never use limestone as grit because it dissolves; use hard stones. You can buy grit or make your own by crushing clean bricks or stones with a hammer. Sieve to get right size. Provide a handful per 10 birds per week. For quail, use a shallow dish; they need less. If birds are on concrete, they need grit. If free-range, they may find stones, but still offer some. Calcium is critical for eggshells. Laying guinea fowl and quail need 3-4% calcium in their diet. The best source is crushed limestone or oyster shells. You can also use crushed eggshells from your kitchen. Bake eggshells at 200Â°C for 10 minutes to kill bacteria, then crush. Offer calcium free choice in a separate feeder. Do not mix into feed for layers because they may overeat. For guinea fowl, provide 5 g per bird per day. For quail, 2 g per bird per day. If eggshells are thin or soft, increase calcium. If birds eat too much calcium, they may get kidney problems; so keep it separate. Also, vitamin D3 is needed for calcium absorption. Ensure your premix has D3, or expose birds to sunlight. In hot climates, provide shade but allow morning sun. For quail in cages, use a vitamin D3 supplement in water once a week. A simple test: collect eggs and check shell thickness. Strong shells break with difficulty. Weak shells crack easily. Adjust calcium accordingly. Never use gypsum or plaster as calcium; it is not digestible. Use only feed-grade limestone or oyster shells. For small flocks, you can make a calcium feeder from a plastic bottle with holes. Hang it at bird height. Refill weekly. Grit and calcium are cheap but vital. Without them, you lose eggs and money. So always keep both available. This is one of the easiest ways to improve productivity.

lessons.title: Water Management: Clean Water Systems for Healthy Birds
lessons.body: Clean water is the most important nutrient. Birds can survive days without feed but not without water. Guinea fowl and quail need fresh, clean water daily. A single bird drinks: chicks 50 ml per day, growers 100 ml, layers 200-250 ml. For 100 guinea fowl, you need 25 liters per day. For 100 quail, 5 liters per day. In hot weather, double these amounts. Use proper waterers: for chicks, use shallow dishes with marbles or stones to prevent drowning. For adults, use hanging drinkers or nipple systems. Nipple drinkers are best: they keep water clean and reduce disease. You can make a simple nipple drinker from a bucket with poultry nipples. For quail, use small cup drinkers. Never use open troughs; birds defecate in them. Clean waterers daily with soap and water, then rinse well. Once a week, disinfect with chlorine solution (1 teaspoon per 4 liters). Let dry before refilling. Position waterers away from feeders to keep feed dry. Also, raise waterers as birds grow; keep at back height. In hot climates, place waterers in shade. Add ice blocks on very hot days. Check water level twice daily; refill as needed. If water is dirty, birds drink less and get sick. Signs of dehydration: dull eyes, ruffled feathers, reduced eating. If you see this, give water with electrolytes (1 teaspoon salt, 1 teaspoon sugar, 1 liter water) for 2 days. For quail, use a shallow dish with a wire cover to keep them out. Always provide water before feed in the morning. A good system: for every 50 birds, have 2 waterers. For quail, 4 small drinkers per 100 birds. Clean water reduces disease and improves egg production. Also, water helps regulate body temperature. In Africa, where heat is common, water management is critical. Never let waterers run dry. If you go away, ensure someone checks. Use rainwater if clean, but filter it. Well water is good but test for salt. If salty, use alternative. Always store water in clean containers. This simple practice will keep your birds healthy and productive. So invest in good waterers and clean them daily.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Feeding Guinea Fowl and Quail with Local Ingredients

Feeding is the single largest recurring cost in guinea fowl and quail production â typically 60â75% of total operating expenses. For African smallholders and emerging commercial producers, the profit margin lives or dies on how well you convert locally available feedstuffs into eggs and meat. This practical reference consolidates the essentials: what your birds need at each stage, how to mix rations from maize, soya, fish meal and local supplements, how to use kitchen waste and by-products safely, feeding schedules, grit and calcium, and water management. Treat it as your daily operating manual.

1. Nutritional Needs at Different Ages

Guinea fowl and quail are not chickens. They have higher protein requirements, especially in the first weeks, and quail â being tiny â need fine particle sizes and higher energy density per gram. Guinea keets are vigorous foragers but still need a balanced starter. Japanese quail mature in 6â7 weeks and start laying at 6â8 weeks, so the transition from starter to layer feed happens fast.

Table 1: Recommended nutrient levels for guinea fowl and Japanese quail by age (as-fed basis)
Bird & age Crude protein (%) Metabolisable energy (kcal/kg) Calcium (%) Key notes
Guinea keets, 0â4 weeks 24â28 2,800â3,000 0.9â1.1 Fine crumble; high protein for rapid growth
Guinea growers, 5â12 weeks 20â22 2,700â2,900 1.0 Transition to pellets; allow foraging
Guinea layers/breeders 17â19 2,700â2,800 2.5â3.5 Calcium critical for shell quality
Quail chicks, 0â3 weeks 26â28 2,900â3,100 0.9â1.0 Very fine crumble; high energy
Quail growers, 4â6 weeks 22â24 2,800â3,000 1.0 Prepare for onset of lay
Quail layers/breeders 20â22 2,800â3,000 2.5â3.0 Also needs 0.3â0.4% available phosphorus

Sources: FAO Guinea Fowl Production and Quail Production Systems technical guides; NRC Nutrient Requirements of Poultry (1994) adapted for tropical smallholder conditions.

2. Mixing Your Own Feed Using Local Ingredients

Commercial feed is convenient but expensive and often unavailable in rural areas. A well-formulated home mix using maize, soya, fish meal and local supplements can cut feed cost by 30â50% while maintaining performance. The key is consistency in ingredients and accurate weighing â use a scale, not a tin.

Table 2: Example home-mixed rations (parts by weight) for guinea fowl and quail in Africa
Ingredient Guinea starter (%) Guinea layer (%) Quail starter (%) Quail layer (%)
Maize (ground) 45 55 42 50
Soya bean meal (full-fat or solvent) 25 18 30 22
Fish meal (60â65% CP) 12 8 14 10
Wheat bran / rice bran 10 12 6 8
Limestone / oyster shell 1 5 1 4.5
Local supplements (leaf meal, Moringa, termites, etc.) 5 1.5 5 4.5
Salt + premix 2 0.5 2 1

Sources: FAO Feed from Local Resources; ILRI smallholder poultry feed formulation guidelines; adapted from practical West African feed trials.

3. Using Kitchen Waste and Farm By-Products Safely

Kitchen waste and farm by-products â cassava peels, banana pseudostems, brewers' spent grain, vegetable trimmings, termites, snails â can supply 10â30% of feed needs and reduce costs. But they carry real risks: mycotoxins, pathogens, toxins (e.g. raw cassava cyanide), and nutritional imbalance. Always cook or ferment high-risk materials, dry thoroughly, and never let waste exceed 20% of the ration for layers.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Never Feed These to Guinea Fowl or Quail

  • Mouldy maize or groundnut â aflatoxins cause liver damage, drop in egg production and sudden death.
  • Raw cassava peels or leaves â contain cyanogenic glycosides; must be sun-dried or fermented for at least 48 hours before use.
  • Rotten meat, fish or kitchen scraps â botulism and salmonella risk; cook thoroughly or avoid.
  • Avocado, raw potato, tomato leaves, onion, garlic in large amounts â toxic to poultry.
  • Salty or oily leftovers â excess salt causes kidney failure; rancid oil causes vitamin E deficiency.

4. Feeding Schedules: How Much and How Often

Guinea fowl are grazers and need less concentrate than quail, which are kept intensively. Feed intake also depends on body weight, temperature and production stage. Below are practical daily allowances per bird. Split into two feeds (morning and late afternoon) to reduce waste and improve digestion.

  • Guinea keets (0â4 weeks): 15â25 g/bird/day, in shallow feeders, 3â4 times daily.
  • Guinea growers (5â12 weeks): 40â60 g/bird/day, plus free-range foraging.
  • Guinea layers: 70â90 g/bird/day, plus grit and greens.
  • Quail chicks (0â3 weeks): 5â8 g/bird/day, 3 times daily.
  • Quail growers (4â6 weeks): 12â18 g/bird/day.
  • Quail layers: 20â28 g/bird/day; do not overfeed â obesity cuts egg production.

Always provide feed in clean, shallow troughs. For quail, use chick feeders with lips to prevent spillage. Remove stale feed daily.

5. Providing Grit and Calcium for Strong Eggshells

Guinea fowl and quail need insoluble grit (small stones) in the gizzard to grind feed, and soluble calcium (limestone, oyster shell) for eggshell formation. Calcium deficiency leads to soft-shelled eggs, thin shells, and bone weakness in layers.

  • Offer insoluble grit (clean river sand or crushed granite, 2â4 mm) free-choice in a separate hopper.
  • Offer oyster shell or limestone free-choice, especially from onset of lay.
  • For quail, crush oyster shell to 1â2 mm so they can swallow it.
  • Do not mix grit into the feed â keep separate to allow self-regulation.

6. Water Management: Clean Water Systems for Healthy Birds

Water is the most overlooked nutrient. Birds drink 1.5â2 times their feed weight daily; in hot African conditions, up to 3 times. Dirty water spreads coccidiosis, colibacillosis and salmonella. Clean water systems are cheap insurance.

  • Provide clean, cool water at all times â never let drinkers run dry.
  • Use nipple drinkers or narrow-mouth fountains to keep water free of droppings.
  • Wash drinkers daily with clean water and scrub weekly with a mild disinfectant.
  • Raise drinkers on a platform to prevent litter and dirt entering.
  • In hot weather, add electrolytes or a pinch of sugar to reduce heat stress.
  • For quail, use shallow drinkers with marbles or stones to prevent drowning of chicks.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Match protein level to bird age â 24â28% for keets/chicks, 17â22% for layers.
  • â Weigh ingredients â never guess; use a scale for every mix.
  • â Dry all grains and by-products to below 12% moisture before storage.
  • â Keep kitchen waste under 20% of the ration and cook or ferment risky items.
  • â Feed twice daily; remove stale feed every morning.
  • â Provide free-choice grit and oyster shell in separate hoppers.
  • â Clean drinkers daily; never allow algae or droppings in water.
  • â Store mixed feed in raised, dry, sealed containers; use within 14 days.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Good Practices for Small-Scale Poultry Feed Production (free PDF)
  • FAO â Guinea Fowl Production (free online guide)
  • FAO â Quail Production Systems (free online guide)
  • ILRI â Smallholder Poultry Feed Resources and Formulation Guidelines
  • NRC â Nutrient Requirements of Poultry (reference tables)

Business bottom line: Every kilogram of feed you mix correctly from local ingredients is money kept in your pocket. Track feed cost per egg and per kilogram of live weight weekly. A 10% improvement in feed conversion is often the difference between a loss-making and a profitable guinea fowl or quail enterprise.

quiz.q: What is the recommended protein level for guinea fowl starter feed (0-4 weeks)?
quiz.explanation: Starter feed for guinea fowl chicks needs 24-28% protein for rapid growth.

quiz.q: At what age do quail typically start laying eggs?
quiz.explanation: Quail mature quickly and start laying at around 6 weeks of age.

quiz.q: Which ingredient is a good local replacement for fish meal in feed mixing?
quiz.explanation: Dried termites are about 40% protein and can replace fish meal.

quiz.q: What percentage of a 50 kg layer feed mix should be limestone powder?
quiz.explanation: Layer feed typically contains 10% limestone for calcium.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid feeding moldy maize to poultry?
options: C) It has too much protein
quiz.explanation: Moldy maize contains aflatoxins, which are toxic to birds.

quiz.q: What is a safe maximum proportion of kitchen waste in a bird's daily diet?
quiz.explanation: Kitchen waste should not exceed 30% of daily feed to avoid nutrient gaps.

quiz.q: Which of these kitchen scraps is toxic to guinea fowl and quail?
quiz.explanation: Avocado contains persin, which is toxic to birds.

quiz.q: How should farm by-products like cassava peels be prepared before feeding?
options: B) Dried in sun for 2 days
quiz.explanation: Sun-drying kills mold and parasites, making by-products safe.

quiz.q: For 100 laying guinea fowl, how much feed is needed per day?
quiz.explanation: Laying guinea fowl eat about 100-120 g each, so 100 birds need 10-12 kg daily.

quiz.q: How many meals per day are recommended for quail chicks (1-2 weeks old)?
quiz.explanation: Quail chicks should be fed 3 small meals daily for better digestion.

quiz.q: What is a sign that you are overfeeding your birds?
quiz.explanation: Leftover feed after 20 minutes indicates overfeeding.

quiz.q: In hot weather, when is the best time to feed guinea fowl?
options: B) Early morning and late evening
quiz.explanation: Feeding during cooler hours reduces heat stress and improves intake.

quiz.q: What size grit should adult guinea fowl receive?
quiz.explanation: Adult guinea fowl need grit of 3-5 mm to grind food in the gizzard.

quiz.q: Why should limestone not be used as grit?
options: B) It dissolves in the gizzard
quiz.explanation: Limestone dissolves and cannot function as grit for grinding.

quiz.q: How can you make eggshells safe to feed as calcium?
quiz.explanation: Baking eggshells kills bacteria like Salmonella.

quiz.q: What is the daily calcium requirement for a laying guinea fowl?
quiz.explanation: Laying guinea fowl need about 5 g of calcium per day for strong shells.

quiz.q: Which vitamin is needed for calcium absorption in birds?
quiz.explanation: Vitamin D3 helps birds absorb calcium from the gut.

quiz.q: How much water does a laying guinea fowl drink per day?
quiz.explanation: Laying guinea fowl drink 200-250 ml of water daily.

quiz.q: What is the best type of drinker to keep water clean for quail?
quiz.explanation: Nipple drinkers prevent contamination and reduce disease.

quiz.q: How often should waterers be cleaned?
quiz.explanation: Daily cleaning with soap and water keeps water free of pathogens.

quiz.q: What is a sign of dehydration in birds?
options: B) Dull eyes and ruffled feathers
quiz.explanation: Dull eyes and ruffled feathers indicate dehydration.

quiz.q: What is the correct chlorine solution for disinfecting waterers?
quiz.explanation: A mild chlorine solution of 1 teaspoon per 4 liters is safe for disinfection.

quiz.q: For 100 quail, how many liters of water are needed daily?
quiz.explanation: Quail drink about 50 ml each, so 100 quail need 5 liters per day.

quiz.q: What should you do if water is very salty from a well?
quiz.explanation: Salty water can harm birds, so use a different clean water source.

quiz.q: How much starter feed does a guinea fowl chick eat per day in week 1-4?
quiz.explanation: Guinea fowl chicks eat about 30 g of starter feed daily.

quiz.q: What is the protein level for quail grower feed (6 weeks onward)?
quiz.explanation: Quail grower feed should have 20% protein after 6 weeks.

quiz.q: Which local supplement can provide vitamins in feed?
quiz.explanation: Moringa leaves are rich in vitamins and can be added at 5% of mix.

quiz.q: Why should you not feed raw meat to poultry?
quiz.explanation: Raw meat can carry pathogens that cause disease in birds.

quiz.q: How often should you provide grit to guinea fowl?
quiz.explanation: Grit should be offered free choice, but a handful per 10 birds weekly is sufficient.

quiz.q: What is a good way to test if eggshells are strong?
quiz.explanation: Gently squeezing eggs helps assess shell strength; weak shells crack easily.
